patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Igloolik (Nunavut) → Belgium: Fr Eric Dejaeger (fugitive 1995–2011).
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Marc Dutroux: first report 1995, first action 1996 (1 years). His mother wrote to authorities in 1995 that he was holding two girls; police took 14 months to arrest him although he was a prime suspect from June 1995; earlier released on parole after three years of a 1989 sentence
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 1998: Dutroux parliamentary commission of inquiry (Verwilghen Commission).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 1 documented adoption flows into Belgium on this map.
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: State-backed adoption systems that falsified children's papers
patterns.role_note: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role_note: Dutroux 'X-dossiers' — witness claims of an elite abuse network (claimed, not established).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect networks that abuse children circulate widely. The records gathered for this map show a few cases where a state service was involved, several claims that investigations found to be false, and some that remain unproven. In Chile, Paul Schäfer, who founded the German settlement Colonia Dignidad in 1961, was convicted in 2006 of abusing children there; Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship used the settlement to torture its opponents, and Germany admitted in 2016 that its embassy had failed to act. In West Berlin, from the late 1960s, the city's youth authorities placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler. In Afghanistan, US soldiers were told not to intervene when Afghan commanders allied with them abused boys. In Bosnia around 2001, UN police monitors and employees of a US contractor bought women and girls who had been trafficked. In the United States and Australia, police took over websites used to share abuse images and kept them running for weeks or months to identify the users. Investigations found no evidence that MI5 used the Kincora boys' home in Belfast for blackmail, and the ring of powerful men that London police investigated in Operation Midland was invented by Carl Beech, who was later jailed. The claim that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency has not been established.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Flanders — historical abuse in youth institutions and boarding schools, parliamentary apology; Dutroux affair — kidnap, abuse and murder of girls; police and justice failures; Belgium — Chamber special committee on sexual abuse in the Church (Lalieux, 2011); Belgian Chamber commission of inquiry on sexual abuse in the Church after 'Godvergeten' (2024).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

patterns.pattern: False alarms that drown real cases
patterns.role_note: Dutroux 'X-dossiers' — witness claims of an elite abuse network.
patterns.pattern_summary: False stories about child trafficking take police time and public attention away from real cases. In July 2020 a claim spread online that the furniture company Wayfair was selling children through its listings. The US National Human Trafficking Hotline received hundreds of reports about it within days, and Polaris, the charity that runs the hotline, said the volume made it harder to help people who needed help; none of the reports contained new information. In 2016 a false claim known as "Pizzagate", that a Washington pizza restaurant was the centre of a child-abuse ring, led a man to fire a rifle inside the restaurant. In London, the Metropolitan Police spent more than £2 million on Operation Midland, which investigated claims made by Carl Beech about a ring of powerful men; the claims were false, Beech was jailed for perverting the course of justice, and he had separately admitted child sexual offences. In the 1980s the McMartin preschool case in California, built on claims of ritual abuse, cost about $14 million and ended without a conviction.

cases.title: Dutroux affair — kidnap, abuse and murder of girls; police and justice failures
cases.who: Marc Dutroux, Michelle Martin, Michel Lelièvre; Belgian Gendarmerie and judicial police
cases.what: Dutroux, on parole for earlier rapes, kidnapped six girls aged 8 to 19 in 1995–96; he was found guilty of kidnapping and raping all six, killing two and causing the deaths of two others. He was arrested in August 1996, and in October 1996 hundreds of thousands of Belgians joined the White March in Brussels to protest police and judicial failures. A parliamentary inquiry chaired by Marc Verwilghen sharply criticised the police investigation. On 22 June 2004 Dutroux was sentenced to life; his ex-wife Michelle Martin got 30 years and Michel Lelièvre 25; businessman Michel Nihoul was acquitted of kidnapping and conspiracy but convicted of drug trafficking and other crimes (five years). Belgium later reorganised its police forces.
cases.cover_up: Dutroux was released early in 1992 from a 13.5-year sentence over prosecutor and psychiatrist objections. Police missed chances, including voices heard in his cellar and unreviewed videotapes; rivalry between Gendarmerie and judicial police hampered the hunt. Judge Connerotte was removed in Oct 1996 for attending a victims' fundraising dinner.

cases.title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
cases.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
cases.what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

cases.title: Fr Eric Dejaeger — Oblate in Nunavut
cases.who: Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate; Belgian-born Fr Eric Dejaeger
cases.what: Belgian-born Oblate missionary Eric Dejaeger had served a five-year sentence in the early 1990s for 11 counts of sexual and indecent assault against children in Baker Lake, Nunavut. When charged over Igloolik he fled to Belgium, where he lived in Oblate homes for 16 years despite an international warrant; Oblate officials acknowledged they knew he was about to leave. Returned to Canada in 2011, he was convicted on 12 September 2014 of 24 further counts, and with eight guilty pleas was sentenced in 2015 for 32 sex crimes against Inuit children in Igloolik between 1978 and 1982. He received 19 years (eight after time served); appeals were dismissed in 2018.

cases.title: Adriaenssens commission and Vangheluwe resignation, Belgium
cases.who: Catholic Church in Belgium, about 29 religious orders; Bishop Roger Vangheluwe of Bruges
cases.what: Bishop Roger Vangheluwe of Bruges resigned in April 2010 after admitting he abused his nephew from 1973 to 1986. The church-backed commission led by psychiatrist Peter Adriaenssens received 475 complaints in six months; its report of 10 September 2010 recorded 13 suicides linked to clerical abuse and 102 verified alleged abusers in about 29 orders. In June 2010 police raided church premises and seized the commission's files (Operation Chalice/Kelk); an appeals court later ruled the raids disproportionate.
cases.cover_up: Judicial raid in June 2010 seized the commission's files (later ruled disproportionate); commission members resigned

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: Belgium — Chamber special committee on sexual abuse in the Church (Lalieux, 2011)
cases.who: Catholic Church in Belgium; Belgian justice system
cases.what: After the June 2010 police raids that ended the Adriaenssens commission, the Belgian Chamber set up a special committee on the handling of sexual abuse in relationships of authority, especially within the Church, chaired by Karine Lalieux. Its report, approved unanimously on 30 March 2011, found abuse in every sector of the church and across the country, especially in Catholic boarding schools, with families reporting at least 13 suicides. It recommended an independent arbitration body for compensation and extending the limitation period from 10 to 15 years after a victim turns 18. The arbitration centre and its compensation scheme followed in 2012.

cases.title: Belgium (Flanders) — expert panel and Ethiopia investigation on intercountry adoption malpractice
cases.who: Flemish adoption services; intermediaries in Ethiopia and other countries of origin
cases.what: After reports of malpractice in adoptions from Ethiopia in 2019, the Flemish government appointed an independent expert panel on intercountry adoption, which delivered its findings in 2021 (final report dated 15 February 2023), and funded the Flemish Centre for Adoption to examine Ethiopian adoptions from 1997 to 2015. Preliminary conclusions found that the true story sometimes differed from the adoption files and that in the worst cases children had not been given up voluntarily by their birth parents. The panel's report led to screening of every country of origin, after which Flanders stopped adoptions from Vietnam and then from Gambia, Haiti and Morocco.

cases.title: Belgian Chamber commission of inquiry on sexual abuse in the Church after 'Godvergeten' (2024)
cases.who: Catholic Church in Belgium; Belgian justice system
cases.what: The federal Chamber set up a parliamentary commission of inquiry into sexual abuse in the Church and elsewhere, chaired by Sophie De Wit (N-VA), after the 2023 VRT series 'Godvergeten'. Its final report of 2 May 2024 made 137 recommendations, including that the Church proactively trace perpetrators through its archives and give police and courts access to relevant church files, and a legal study on retroactively ending the limitation period for child sexual abuse. It called for reducing the 58% of sexual-violence cases dismissed by prosecutors, and for a new inquiry into the 2010 'Operation Kelk' investigation after the High Council of Justice reported dysfunctions. It proposed an abuse commissioner, a centre of expertise and an arbitration body for time-barred cases.
cases.cover_up: The commission noted 58% of cases are dismissed by prosecutors and called for a new inquiry into the 2010 'Operation Kelk' raids after the High Council of Justice reported dysfunctions.

cases.title: Belgium — Halsberghe commission (2000) and convictions
cases.who: Catholic Church in Belgium
cases.what: A church commission chaired by Godelieve Halsberghe from 2000 received over 300 complaints and upheld 32 of 33 formal ones; 31 were time-barred. Convictions included Fr Bruno Vos (nine years in 2009 for raping four minors), Robert Borremans (five years, 2008) and two Brothers jailed for ten years each in 2005 for abusing disabled people. On 24 June 2010 police raided the archbishop's palace in Mechelen, seizing 450 dossiers, and searched Cardinal Danneels' residence.
cases.cover_up: In about half the 32 upheld cases the accused refused to appear; 31 cases were time-barred and only one reached court; in June 2010 police seized 450 internal dossiers from the Mechelen archbishop's palace

cases.title: Flanders — historical abuse in youth institutions and boarding schools, parliamentary apology
cases.who: Flemish youth institutions, youth centres and boarding schools
cases.what: After clergy abuse cases, further cases emerged of child abuse in Flemish institutions between 1930 and 1990. A working group of experts led by child psychiatrist Peter Adriaenssens, set up by Welfare Minister Jo Vandeurzen, produced two reports recognising the wide scope of abuse. On 23 April 2014 Flemish Parliament Speaker Jan Peumans formally apologised to victims of abuse in boarding schools and youth centres. A temporary recognition and mediation commission set up in 2014 was later made permanent; it received 121 reports in 2024.

cases.title: Operation Gargamel — Belgian-led investigation of 9 million files
cases.who: Offenders producing their own abuse material
cases.what: Belgian federal judicial police found more than 9 million images and videos, mostly never seen before, in a house search. With Europol victim-identification taskforces, 90 suspects (24 in Belgium) and 110 victims were identified by March 2020; an Australian suspect was sentenced to 15 years. Police in over 40 countries received intelligence packages.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

cases.title: Europol sprint on buyers of live-distant abuse in the Philippines (2024)
cases.who: Buyers worldwide directing livestreamed abuse by traffickers in the Philippines
cases.what: From 24 to 28 June 2024, 32 investigators at Europol processed leads from US HSI investigations into networks exploiting children in the Philippines: over 10 million lines of chat between about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 seller accounts, built up over 12 years. The sprint produced information packages that may lead authorities in 24 countries to 197 buyers. Europol notes buyers direct traffickers to abuse children in real time on webcam and some travel to the Philippines to abuse children in person.

cases.title: EU Child Sexual Abuse Regulation ('chat control') and interim derogation
cases.who: European Commission, Council and Parliament
cases.what: The Commission proposed the CSA Regulation (COM(2022) 209) to require platforms to assess risks and allow detection orders; it has been deadlocked over mandatory scanning. The interim derogation from the ePrivacy Directive (Regulation (EU) 2021/1232, in force 2 August 2021, extended in 2024) let providers voluntarily detect abuse material; with no agreement it lapsed on 3 April 2026. A new temporary derogation, Regulation (EU) 2026/1881, was adopted on 24 July 2026 and published 28 July 2026. As of October 2026 the permanent regulation has not been adopted.

cases.title: Dutroux 'X-dossiers' — witness claims of an elite abuse network
cases.who: Witnesses X1–X4 (claims); Belgian prosecutors
cases.what: Witnesses told investigators in 1996–97 of abuse parties and unsolved murders involving Marc Dutroux, Michel Nihoul and prominent people. Prosecutors ultimately dismissed the statements, and investigators were criticised for leading a key witness; an officer charged in 1997 with falsifying her statements was cleared in 1999. In 1999 the Guardian reported renewed cover-up claims, and that the parliamentary inquiry's chair said his findings had been muzzled. The claims of an elite network remain unproven; a 1999 book by three journalists argued the witnesses were more credible than portrayed.

flows.title: Seoul → Belgium
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Belgium; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: Igloolik (Nunavut) → Belgium: Fr Eric Dejaeger (fugitive 1995–2011)
flows.what: About to be charged in 1995, the Oblate fled to Belgium; Oblate officials acknowledged knowing he was leaving, and he lived 16 years in Oblate houses despite an international warrant until returned in 2011. In 2015 he was sentenced to 19 years for 32 offences against Inuit children in Igloolik (1978–82).

networks.name: South Korea's four authorised overseas adoption agencies (Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
networks.what: The four agencies held guardianship over children and sent them abroad under government policy; Holt sent about half (AP). The TRC (March 2025) found agencies met monthly quotas for foreign partners, falsified orphan status and swapped identities, and that the state failed to supervise them. All four were implicated in the petitions (Guardian, 2023).

networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.

networks.name: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
networks.what: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

cases.title: Bolivia — two former Jesuit provincials convicted for not reporting Fr Alfonso Pedrajas (2025)
cases.who: Society of Jesus (Jesuits), Bolivian province
cases.what: On 2 September 2025 a Bolivian court sentenced Marcos Recolons and Ramón Alaix, Jesuit provincials of Bolivia in 1993–1999 and 1999–2007, to one year in prison each, plus costs, compensation to victims and psychological treatment, for knowing of allegations against Fr Alfonso Pedrajas and not reporting them. Prosecutors presented 18 victims' complaints and 34 witnesses and said they would pursue other priests named at trial. Sentences under three years are normally commuted in Bolivia.
cases.cover_up: The court found the provincials knew of allegations against Pedrajas and did not report them to police; prosecutors seized internal Jesuit documents in La Paz and Cochabamba in May 2023

cases.title: La Pampa, Madre de Dios — Operación Mercurio 2019 and sex trafficking in mining camps
cases.who: Bar/brothel networks serving illegal gold-mining camps
cases.what: On 19–20 February 2019 more than 1,500 military and police began Operación Mercurio against illegal gold mining in La Pampa, in the Tambopata reserve buffer zone, under a state of emergency. Peru's Women's Minister said the worst crimes, including child sexual exploitation and child labour, had been committed there, and her ministry took in minors and women rescued from trafficking. Reporting in 2022 said police were still dismantling networks recruiting women to La Pampa bars; a 16-year-old girl previously rescued from a La Pampa trafficking band was found murdered at km 108 in April 2021.

cases.title: Bolivia — foreign offenders in Indigenous communities near Rurrenabaque (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Foreign offenders; parents; online abuse-material producers
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says foreign offenders exploited children in rural Indigenous communities in northern La Paz department, in and around Rurrenabaque and Santa Cruz, and in tourist areas of La Paz and Beni; production of abuse material for sale online is rising in Cochabamba, El Alto and Santa Cruz; and Bolivian women and girls are exploited in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Panama and Peru. Tren de Aragua is reported to be involved in trafficking in Bolivia.
