networks.name: Legion of Christ (Legionaries of Christ)
networks.what: Founded in Mexico in 1941 by Marcial Maciel. The Vatican said in 2010 that Maciel committed 'true crimes' and the Legion had shielded him, and placed it under a papal delegate. The Legion's December 2019 report acknowledged 175 minors abused 1941–2019, 60 by Maciel and the rest by 33 priests.

networks.name: Marist Brothers
networks.what: Teaching order founded in France. Listed 154 members accused in Australia (1980–2015); nine Brothers convicted in New Zealand; apologised for systemic abuse at Scottish schools; acknowledged at least 14 victims of one Brother in Chile; complaints against 12 teachers at Barcelona schools.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 1998: Commission on Human Rights and Administrative Justice (CHRAJ) on Trokosi.
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found West and Central Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Trokosi — ritual servitude of girls at shrines
cases.who: Traditional shrines (Ewe in Ghana and Togo; Fon in Benin)
cases.what: Under trokosi, shrines take girls, usually young virgins, as atonement for a relative's alleged wrongdoing; they serve priests without pay, and in most shrines sexual service to the priest is treated as a duty, which defenders deny. Ghana amended its Criminal Code in 1998 to make ritual or customary servitude a crime with a minimum three-year sentence, but the practice continued and no prosecutions are recorded in the source.

cases.title: Nigeria — Kaduna 'Islamic school' raid frees 300+ boys and men
cases.who: Imam Ahmad Bun Hambal Centre for Islamic Studies (purported Islamic school / rehabilitation centre)
cases.what: On 26 September 2019 Kaduna police raided a building signed as an Islamic studies centre and freed more than 300 boys and men, many chained and with whip scars. Some had been brought from Burkina Faso, Mali and Ghana; families said they were denied access. Seven people claiming to be teachers were arrested. Local media reported captives were tortured, starved and sexually abused. The raid led to further rescues from similar 'torture houses' in northern Nigeria.

cases.title: 'Sweetie' sting — 20,000 offers to pay for webcam abuse
cases.who: Terre des hommes Netherlands (virtual 10-year-old 'Sweetie')
cases.what: In a 10-week investigation run from a warehouse in Amsterdam, Terre des hommes Netherlands posed in public chatrooms as 'Sweetie', a computer-generated 10-year-old Filipina girl, to show the scale of webcam child sex abuse: 20,000 internet users offered to pay for webcam sex performances. The researchers identified about 1,000 of them, from 65 countries, including 110 in the UK and 254 traced to computers in the US, and on 4 November 2013 handed their details to Interpol. They said online child exploitation had become a hardened criminal industry in the Philippines.

cases.title: Lake Volta, Ghana — child trafficking in fishing (IJM prevalence study 2023)
cases.who: Fishing-boat owners and intermediaries on Lake Volta
cases.what: A 2023 International Justice Mission household survey of 1,286 children in three fishing districts around Lake Volta estimated that about 37.7 per cent were likely trafficked and a further 45.1 per cent were in likely exploitative child labour. The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit children as young as four in Lake Volta's fishing industry, controlling them with violence and limited food, and that girls in the fishing sector are vulnerable to sexual exploitation; it notes observers reported forced child labour on the lake has decreased.

networks.name: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
networks.what: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role_note: Filed 15-16 Jan 2019 after Guam's 2016 permanent window; claims rose to nearly 280; Jan 2020 plan offered $21m; sold Yona property for $6.1m. Former Archbishop Anthony Apuron found guilty in a canonical trial (2018-19).
patterns.pattern_summary: Most people abused as children do not tell anyone for many years. In many countries and US states the legal deadline for suing or prosecuting, called a statute of limitations, used to run out in a person's early twenties, before most had spoken. When legislatures proposed extending these deadlines or reopening old claims, the institutions that would face lawsuits lobbied against the changes. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million on lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018. In Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference spent more than $7.6 million and the state's insurance federation nearly $20.7 million on lobbying from 2014 to 2024. These totals cover all the issues they lobbied on, not only this one. Where the deadlines were lifted anyway, many institutions filed for bankruptcy. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders did so, several of them hours or days before a trial, a deposition or a new law took effect. The Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics also filed.

cases.title: Archdiocese of Agaña — Archbishop Apuron and bankruptcy
cases.who: Archdiocese of Agaña; former Archbishop Anthony Apuron
cases.what: A Vatican tribunal of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith found former Archbishop Anthony Apuron guilty of some charges including sexual abuse of minors in March 2018; the appeal was rejected in February 2019. He was barred from office and from living in Guam but not laicised; he denies the allegations. The archdiocese filed for bankruptcy in January 2019 facing more than 200 lawsuits naming 35 clergy, teachers and scoutmasters. Guam lifted the civil statute of limitations in 2016.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Ireland → United States: Fr Brendan Smyth.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Holy See and the Murphy Commission (Ireland): No Vatican files supplied
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2018: scandal: Tusla refers 126 illegal birth registrations by St Patrick's Guild (May)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: State-backed adoption systems that falsified children's papers
patterns.role_note: Ireland — Mother and Baby Homes Commission: 9,000 child deaths; adoptions abroad.
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 2017: Ireland: Criminal Law (Sexual Offences) Act 2017 gives worldwide jurisdiction over Irish offenders
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Ireland — Mother and Baby Homes Commission: 9,000 child deaths; adoptions abroad; Ryan Commission — state-funded industrial schools and reformatories, Ireland; Mother and Baby Homes Commission — Ireland; Ireland — illegal birth registrations: St Patrick's Guild (126 cases) and the 2021 sampling review; Ferns Report — Diocese of Ferns; Murphy Report — Archdiocese of Dublin; Ryan Commission — industrial schools run by religious orders.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Fr Brendan Smyth — Norbertine order
cases.who: Norbertine order (Kilnacrott Abbey); Fr Brendan Smyth
cases.what: Norbertine priest Brendan Smyth abused children for decades from the 1950s in Northern Ireland, the Republic and the United States; the BBC put the number at at least 143. In 1975 Seán Brady, later Cardinal, attended church meetings where two teenage victims were sworn to secrecy; their evidence was never given to police. The Irish government's delay in acting on the RUC's extradition request led to the collapse of the Reynolds coalition in 1994. He was jailed in Northern Ireland in 1994 for abusing dozens of children there, and in July 1997 was sentenced in Dublin to 12 years for abusing 20 children in the Republic. He died in the Curragh Prison in August 1997. The Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry (2017) found the Norbertine order moved him to another diocese despite knowing his history.
cases.cover_up: Norbertines moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries without reporting him; at a 1975 church inquiry two boys signed oaths of silence; mishandled extradition by the Irish Attorney General's office contributed to the fall of the government in 1994

cases.title: Diocese of Raphoe — Fr Eugene Greene
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Raphoe
cases.what: Fr Eugene Greene, the most notorious offender in the Diocese of Raphoe, was sentenced in 1999 to 12 years in prison for abusing 26 boys over 20 years. A church safeguarding review published on 30 November 2011 found allegations against 14 Raphoe priests between 1975 and 2010, four of whom had been convicted, and pointed to 'significant errors of judgement' by successive bishops. Former bishop Séamus Hegarty said his past practice was 'sometimes poor' and apologised.

cases.title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
cases.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cases.what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

cases.title: Freedom Hosting — Tor host for Lolita City and other abuse sites
cases.who: Freedom Hosting (Eric Eoin Marques, convicted)
cases.what: Freedom Hosting was a free anonymous dark web hosting service that ran from July 2008 to July 2013 and hosted over 200 child exploitation websites, including Lolita City, which Anonymous had attacked in 2011. The operator, Eric Eoin Marques, was arrested in Dublin in early August 2013 on a US warrant; the FBI accused him of being 'the largest facilitator of child porn on the planet'. After Ireland's Supreme Court dismissed his challenge in March 2019 he was extradited, pleaded guilty on 6 February 2020 to conspiracy to advertise child sexual abuse material, and on 16 September 2021 was sentenced to 27 years. DOJ said the sites held millions of images and videos, over 1.97 million not previously known to law enforcement.
cases.cover_up: Extradition from Ireland took from 2013 to 2019 through appeals.

cases.title: Landslide Productions / Operations Avalanche and Ore
cases.who: Landslide Productions (payment portal, Thomas and Janice Reedy)
cases.what: Landslide, a Fort Worth, Texas portal run by Thomas and Janice Reedy, processed credit-card sign-ups for third-party sites, some offering child abuse images. US agents raided it in August 1999; a jury convicted Thomas Reedy, who was sentenced to 1,335 years (reduced to 180 on appeal), and Janice Reedy got 14 years. US Operation Avalanche examined about 35,000 names on the database, and the FBI passed details of 7,272 British residents to UK police, starting Operation Ore, Britain's biggest computer crime investigation; raids began in May 2002. CEOP said 140 children had been rescued in the UK. Later forensic examination showed large-scale credit card fraud in Landslide's records (54,348 sets of stolen card details), and some people were wrongly accused; a legal challenge in 2009 argued that many convictions for incitement rested on flawed credit-card evidence. Follow-on operations took place in other countries.
cases.cover_up: Later reconstruction of the Landslide data found many listed names were victims of credit-card fraud, and the validity of UK Operation Ore procedures was questioned; an estimated 33 suicides followed in the UK.

cases.title: Diocese of Stockton — Fr Oliver O'Grady
cases.who: Diocese of Stockton; Bishop Roger Mahony (later Cardinal Archbishop of Los Angeles)
cases.what: Irish-born priest Oliver O'Grady, ordained in 1971 for the Diocese of Stockton, abused children from about 1973 and was moved between parishes. Bishop Roger Mahony knew of concerns by 1980 and moved him in 1984. O'Grady was convicted in 1993 and sentenced to 14 years; a 1998 civil jury awarded $30 million (reduced to $7 million). Paroled and deported to Ireland in 2000, he was convicted there for child abuse images in 2012 and 2020.
cases.cover_up: After police declined to charge him in 1984, Bishop Mahony moved him to another parish and later made him pastor; Mahony said he was unaware of molestation reports, although a letter about earlier abuse was in O'Grady's personnel file.

cases.title: Murphy Report — Archdiocese of Dublin
cases.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Dublin
cases.what: The Commission of Investigation into the Catholic Archdiocese of Dublin reported on 26 November 2009. It examined a representative sample of 46 priests out of 102 within its remit; 320 people complained of child sexual abuse between 1975 and 2004. It found former Archbishops McQuaid, Ryan, McNamara and Connell failed to report what they knew to the Gardaí, and said the archdiocese's move to take out insurance against abuse claims showed it knew abuse was a potential major cost. It also criticised the Gardaí for treating priests as outside their remit; the Garda Commissioner called the report 'difficult and disturbing reading'.
cases.cover_up: Abuse 'covered up' 1975–2004; bishops generally did not report to Gardaí before 1996; archdiocese took out insurance against abuse litigation from 1987; Gardaí knew of complaints against Fr Tony Walsh in 1990–91 and took no action

cases.title: Ireland — illegal birth registrations: St Patrick's Guild (126 cases) and the 2021 sampling review
cases.who: St Patrick's Guild adoption society; Tusla and the Adoption Authority of Ireland (record holders); the Irish state
cases.what: In May 2018 the Irish government announced that 126 people placed through the St Patrick's Guild adoption society had been illegally registered as the birth children of their adoptive parents. An independent review then sampled 1,496 of about 150,000 adoption records; its report, published in March 2021, found about 265 files with suspicious markers and estimated 5,540 to 19,980 files might show similar signs. Tusla reported evidence of coerced consent, children placed abroad with little documentation and altered names and birth dates; the report did not recommend a full file review.

cases.title: Ireland — Murphy inquiry into child sexual abuse in swimming (1998)
cases.who: Irish Amateur Swimming Association (IASA); national coaches including Derry O'Rourke and George Gibney (Gibney never tried)
cases.what: The Irish government asked senior counsel Roderick Murphy to inquire after former Olympic coach Derry O'Rourke was jailed for 12 years for abusing 11 girl swimmers. His 165-page report (1998) found that children had come to believe abuse was a normal part of their training, and a 'total systems failure' in the Irish Amateur Swimming Association. It noted Garda investigations into two other coaches and made more than 100 recommendations; the minister cut the association's funding.
cases.cover_up: The report found 'total systems failure' in the IASA; charges against another coach were dropped after a 1994 judicial review because of delay.

cases.title: Madonna House residential centre, Dublin — Department of Health inquiry (1996)
cases.who: Madonna House children's residential centre, run by the Sisters of Charity
cases.what: The report of the inquiry into Madonna House, a Sisters of Charity residential centre for children in Dublin, was published in 1996 with its most damaging sections removed on legal advice. The withheld sections, revealed in May 1999 after RTÉ's States of Fear team obtained them, described beatings, humiliation and sexual assaults on children by a small number of staff, and management that failed to take effective action on staff concerns and children's complaints.
cases.cover_up: Management failed to act on staff concerns and children's complaints; one staff member regarded as having an inappropriate relationship with a girl was paid to live elsewhere but kept his job; the sections describing abuse were removed from the published 1996 report and only revealed in 1999.

cases.title: Ferns Report — Diocese of Ferns
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Ferns
cases.what: The state Ferns Inquiry, published 25 October 2005, examined more than 100 allegations of child sexual abuse made between 1962 and 2002 against 21 priests of the diocese. Bishop Donal Herlihy moved accused priests temporarily and then reinstated them, and ordained men he knew or should have known posed a risk. Bishop Brendan Comiskey never got a priest to stand aside from ministry. The report found Garda handling of one of eight formal complaints 'wholly inadequate' and some pre-1988 complaints were not recorded.
cases.cover_up: Bishop Herlihy moved accused priests to other posts or dioceses for a period, then reinstated them; Gardaí failed to record or properly investigate some pre-1988 complaints

cases.title: Cloyne Report — Diocese of Cloyne
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Cloyne; Bishop John Magee
cases.what: The Cloyne Report, published 13 July 2011, examined the diocese's handling of allegations against 19 clerics from 1996 to February 2009, after the Irish church had adopted reporting procedures. Nine complaints that should have been reported to the Gardaí were not, and none were reported to the health authorities. Bishop John Magee was found to have shown little interest in applying the guidelines for 12 years. The report said the Vatican's response to the Irish procedures allowed bishops to ignore them.
cases.cover_up: Nine complaints that should have gone to the Gardaí were not reported; none of the 1996–2008 complaints reported to the health service; Vatican's reaction to Irish guidelines described as 'entirely unhelpful'

cases.title: Ryan Commission — industrial schools run by religious orders
cases.who: Christian Brothers (most boys' institutions), Sisters of Mercy (most girls' institutions) and other Catholic orders
cases.what: The Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse reported on 20 May 2009 after a nine-year investigation of more than 250 church-run institutions that held over 30,000 children from the 1930s to the 1990s. It found sexual abuse 'endemic' in boys' institutions run mainly by the Christian Brothers; the Sisters of Mercy ran most girls' institutions. The 2,600-page report names no perpetrators after a Christian Brothers lawsuit. A parallel state redress scheme paid about 12,000 people an average of €65,000.
cases.cover_up: Christian Brothers sued the commission in 2004 to keep members' names out; no real names of perpetrators published; findings not to be used for prosecutions; state Department of Education inspections failed

cases.title: Scoping Inquiry — abuse in religious-run schools
cases.who: 42 religious orders that ran day and boarding schools
cases.what: The state Scoping Inquiry, published 3 September 2024, recorded 2,395 allegations of sexual abuse against 884 alleged abusers at 308 schools run by 42 religious orders, mostly from the 1960s to the 1990s. 590 allegations involving 190 alleged abusers concerned 17 special schools. More than half of the alleged abusers are dead. The government announced a full Commission of Investigation.

cases.title: Ireland — Mother and Baby Homes Commission: 9,000 child deaths; adoptions abroad
cases.who: Religious orders (incl. Bon Secours Sisters), local authorities and the Irish state
cases.what: The Commission of Investigation's final report (published 12 January 2021) covered 14 mother and baby homes and 4 county homes. About 9,000 children died in them between 1922 and 1998, about one in seven births and about twice the general infant mortality rate. Several homes had been linked to illegal domestic and foreign adoptions, many to the United States. On 13 January 2021 Taoiseach Micheál Martin apologised for a 'profound generational wrong'. (The care agent may hold the home-conditions record; this record focuses on removals and adoptions.)
cases.cover_up: In May 2018 Tusla referred 126 cases of births falsely registered by the St Patrick's Guild adoption agency (illegal registrations that hid children's identities).

cases.title: Marcial Maciel and the Legion of Christ — 2019 internal report
cases.who: Legion of Christ (Legionaries); founder Marcial Maciel
cases.what: For decades until 2006 the Vatican dismissed accusations by seminarians that founder Marcial Maciel had abused them. In 2006 it ordered him to retire to a life of 'prayer and penitence', and on 1 May 2010, after an apostolic visitation, it said his acts were 'true crimes'. The Legion's own report, released on 21 December 2019, found that 175 minors were abused by 33 of its priests between 1941 and 2019; at least 60 of them by Maciel. It said 111 of the 175 were victims of Maciel or of his victims, and that 14 of the 33 abusive priests had themselves been abused within the order.
cases.cover_up: Letters to the Vatican in 1976, 1978 and 1989 and formal charges in 1998 produced no action; Vatican in 2010 said the Legion had shielded Maciel; Maciel never laicised or tried

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

cases.title: Scouting Ireland — 'Historical Sexual Abuse in Scouting: A Learning Review' (Elliott)
cases.who: Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland (CBSI) and Scout Association of Ireland (SAI), merged as Scouting Ireland in 2004
cases.what: Child-protection consultant Ian Elliott's 'Historical Sexual Abuse in Scouting: A Learning Review', published by Scouting Ireland on 14 May 2020, found a cover-up and failure to report abuse in the former Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland and Scout Association of Ireland. It described 'a culture driven by self-interest', said 'cronyism thrived', and found that people suspected or known to be sex offenders gained positions of power and became 'largely impregnable'; records had been lost or destroyed, so the full extent could not be determined. An earlier audit reported to the Oireachtas in November 2018 had found evidence of 108 alleged victims and 71 alleged abusers, with numbers expected to rise considerably.
cases.cover_up: The review found 'coverup and a failure to report abuse'; records were lost or destroyed; adults with a sexual interest in young people rose to positions of influence and prevented known offenders being removed.

cases.title: Ireland — National Board's safeguarding reviews of every Catholic diocese and order (2011–2017), incl. Raphoe
cases.who: Catholic dioceses and religious congregations in Ireland and Northern Ireland; National Board for Safeguarding Children in the Catholic Church
cases.what: The Catholic Church's National Board for Safeguarding Children reviewed every diocese on the island of Ireland and the religious orders that ran schools and institutions, publishing in tranches from 30 November 2011 to 2017. The first tranche included Raphoe, where 52 allegations had been made against 14 priests since 1975 and four had been convicted; Bishop Philip Boyce accepted 'very poor judgements and mistakes'. A December 2013 tranche reported, for example, 67 allegations against 21 priests in Kerry and 59 against 42 in Down and Connor.
cases.cover_up: Raphoe: the review found 'significant' errors by bishops, with frequent delays in reporting allegations or none at all, and victims' needs ignored to protect the Church's reputation (Bishop Boyce's statement).

cases.title: Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland — review 2020
cases.who: Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland (with Scout Association of Ireland), now Scouting Ireland
cases.what: A review published in May 2020 found that over several decades before their 2004 merger into Scouting Ireland, the Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland and the Scout Association of Ireland shielded 275 known or suspected abusers. Scouting Ireland accepted the findings and apologised.
cases.cover_up: Organisations shielded known or suspected abusers after abuse was reported

cases.title: Operation Atelier — network of abuse photographers
cases.who: Professional photographers producing abuse material
cases.what: Czech-initiated and supported by Europol and Eurojust: a Czech photographer exploited socially and financially disadvantaged children (close to 70) and, with a Swedish partner, distributed images to customers in the EU and Canada. In 2014 ten people were arrested in the Czech Republic (5), Sweden (2), France, Ireland and Spain; 30 TB of data were seized.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Austria-led 2007 investigation — 2,360 suspects in 77 countries
cases.who: Online distribution network uncovered by Austrian authorities
cases.what: The investigation began in July 2006 when an employee of a Vienna-based file-hosting service reported suspicious material; within 24 hours investigators recorded more than 8,000 hits from 2,361 IP addresses in 77 countries. On 7 February 2007 Austrian authorities announced more than 2,360 suspects who had paid to view videos of young children being sexually abused; the FBI was investigating about 600, about 130 were Australian, France was looking at about 100 and at least 23 were Austrian. Germany had the largest number of suspects. No suspects were yet in custody at the announcement.
cases.cover_up: The two Irish suspects were not investigated by the Garda until six months after Austria notified them.

flows.title: Ireland → United States: Fr Brendan Smyth
flows.what: The Norbertine order knew of Smyth's abuse and moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries, including assignments in the US, sometimes without warning bishops; he abused at least 143 children.

networks.what: National Scout associations; the Boy Scouts of America faced more than 82,000 sexual abuse claims in its 2020 bankruptcy and had kept internal 'ineligible volunteer' files on suspected abusers.

networks.name: Welcome to Video
networks.what: Darknet video site paid in Bitcoin, about 1.2 million members; seized 2018. 337 arrests in 38 countries announced October 2019. Start year 2015 is not in the sources opened and is omitted from cases.

networks.what: Largest Tor web host in 2013, hosting Lolita City and other abuse sites; operator sentenced in the US to 27 years (2021).

networks.what: Irish-founded teaching order. networks.name: Marist Brothers
networks.what: Teaching order founded in France. Listed 154 members accused in Australia (1980–2015); nine Brothers convicted in New Zealand; apologised for systemic abuse at Scottish schools; acknowledged at least 14 victims of one Brother in Chile; complaints against 12 teachers at Barcelona schools.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found Middle East and North Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Jordan and Türkiye — Syrian refugee girls in forced marriages and sex trafficking (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Families and brokers arranging unofficial marriages
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says Syrian girls in Türkiye — which hosted about 2.9 million displaced Syrians — are forced into marriages in unofficial religious ceremonies, particularly in poor rural regions, and then subjected to domestic servitude and sex trafficking. In Jordan, Syrian refugee women and girls have been sold into forced marriages, and in 2022 authorities investigated a mother for allegedly exploiting her two daughters with foreign tourists.
cases.cover_up: Türkiye: no investigations of complicit officials reported, though corruption and complicity remained significant concerns.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Lebanon — Chez Maurice and Silver-B: about 75 Syrian women freed from sex-trafficking ring (2016).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Lebanon — Chez Maurice and Silver-B: about 75 Syrian women freed from sex-trafficking ring (2016)
cases.who: Chez Maurice and Silver-B brothels
cases.what: In March 2016 Lebanese security forces freed as many as 75 Syrian women from two brothels, Chez Maurice and Silver-B, in the Maameltein red-light district of Jounieh, and arrested and indicted over a dozen people on sex-trafficking charges. HRW said Syrian refugee women were at particular risk and that the same premises had been raided in 2011, when a 17-year-old Syrian girl was found, and later reopened. Lebanon's police identified 87 trafficking victims in 2016, mainly these survivors.

flows.title: Syria → Lebanon (refugee women and girls into sex trafficking)
flows.what: Criminal groups recruit Syrian women and girls with false job offers and exploit them in Lebanese brothels; Syrian children held in bonded labour in the Beqaa.

networks.name: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
networks.what: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role_note: : Child sex tourism in Madagascar increased after Mozambique tightened its laws (mostly French and Italian offenders)
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

cases.who: Malagasy and foreign offenders
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says most child sex-trafficking victims are exploited by Malagasy men, but foreign tourists, often from France, also exploit children; parents sometimes encourage daughters into commercial sex with tourists, and children are exploited in Antananarivo karaoke bars. Courts convicted 15 traffickers, the first convictions in four years. A Nosy Be anti-trafficking committee exists. In July 2025 police in Nosy Be arrested two women suspected of filming abuse of their own children and selling the videos to foreign buyers via mobile money (charged; L'Express de Madagascar).

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 1996: Mozambique — Machel study (UN, 1996) on ONUMOZ.
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Mission or crisis zone where children were abused
patterns.role_note: ONUMOZ Mozambique — soldiers recruited girls aged 12–18 into prostitution (Machel study).
patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that Sri Lankan peacekeepers had abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007, and 114 soldiers were sent home; none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014 and 2015; French judges closed the case against the French soldiers in 2018 without charges. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role: Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups
patterns.role_note: Mozambique, Cabo Delgado — abduction of children by ISIS-linked armed groups.
patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. In 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria, and 82 were still captive in 2024. The Lord's Resistance Army abducted children in Uganda and the neighbouring countries over many years; in 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

cases.who: Islamic State–Mozambique Province ('Al-Shabaab' locally) and other armed groups; also Mozambique defence forces (sexual violence, 2023)
cases.what: The UN verified the abduction of 468 children (371 boys, 97 girls) by armed groups in Cabo Delgado in 2024, 392 for recruitment, and sexual violence against 5 girls. cases.title: Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo — Vatican sanctions

The next day the Vatican confirmed it had received allegations in 2019 and imposed disciplinary sanctions in 2020: limits on movement and ministry, no contact with minors and no contact with Timor-Leste. The sanctions were reinforced in 2021. Belo had left Timor in 2002 and worked in Maputo, Mozambique from 2004.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 1,991 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman). 2007: shutdown: Nepal halts all intercountry adoptions (April) after baby-buying reports
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Nepal → India — trafficking of girls to Indian brothels (estimates).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found South Asia lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Nepal — National Human Rights Commission national reports on trafficking: an estimated 5,000 children trafficked in a year
cases.who: Trafficking networks moving women and girls across the open border to India and on to third countries
cases.what: Nepal's National Human Rights Commission, through its Office of the Special Rapporteur on Trafficking in Persons, has published national reports on trafficking since 2005. Its report released in August 2019 estimated that about 35,000 Nepalis were trafficked in 2018, including 5,000 children, and that nearly 1.5 million were at risk. It said nearly 1,000 Nepali women and girls are rescued from India each year and that poor screening at the open border makes cross-border trafficking hard to control. Its 2018 report said girls and women are trafficked to India for prostitution, orchestra dancing, circus work and marriage, and some are moved on to third countries.

cases.title: 'Hidden in Plain Sight' — Australian Parliament recognises orphanage trafficking as modern slavery
cases.who: Australian volunteers, donors, schools and tour operators supporting overseas orphanages
cases.what: The Joint Standing Committee's report 'Hidden in Plain Sight', released on 6 December 2017 from its inquiry into establishing a Modern Slavery Act, recognised orphanage trafficking as a form of modern slavery to be covered by the Act. A chapter was devoted to orphanage trafficking, orphanage tourism and Australian donations, with evidence from ReThink Orphanages, Lumos, the ChildSafe campaign and others. Australia's Modern Slavery Act followed in 2018; Lumos supported the change.

cases.title: SOS Children's Villages — Independent Special Commission (ISC) worldwide report (2023)
cases.who: SOS Children's Villages (federation of member associations; International Senate); former senior staff
cases.what: An Independent Special Commission appointed by the International Senate of SOS Children's Villages in 2021, chaired by former Kenyan Chief Justice Willy Mutunga with former Delhi High Court acting chief justice Gita Mittal, issued its summary report on 6 June 2023. Using a 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard, it confirmed serious allegations of child sexual and physical abuse in several member associations in Africa, Asia and Central America, and found cover-ups of past sexual abuse and failures to report to national authorities in more than one association. Countries named in the report include Nepal, Cambodia, India, Kenya, Panama, Sierra Leone and Syria. A confidential 991-page part two went to the organisation's Senate and Executive Board on 2 May 2023; in November 2025 SOS Children's Villages International said it was examining whether parts could be passed to prosecutors.
cases.cover_up: Former senior staff in some member associations knew of abuse and failed to act or concealed reports; serious abuse was not reported to national authorities.

cases.title: Nepal — Hague Conference mission finds regular falsification of papers to make children 'adoptable' (2010)
cases.who: Child-care homes and intermediaries in Nepal's intercountry adoption system; foreign adoption agencies
cases.what: At the request of Nepal's Ministry of Women, Children and Social Welfare, the Permanent Bureau of the Hague Conference on Private International Law sent a technical assistance mission to Nepal on 23–27 November 2009; its report is dated 4 February 2010. It cited evidence that documents were regularly falsified to declare children adoptable, with false statements about abandonment, origin, age and status, and that this continued under the 2008 rules. It said the USD 5,000 per-child payment and USD 10,000 annual agency fee created strong incentives unrelated to the cost of care, and that Nepal had no data on adoptable children.

cases.title: Kolkata red-light areas — rescues of trafficked Nepali girls and minors (2015, 2025)
cases.who: Brothel keepers and traffickers in Kolkata
cases.what: In January 2015 police, with International Justice Mission and three NGOs, freed six young women trafficked from Nepal from four brothels in Kolkata's largest red-light area; all had fake adult ID documents, which IJM said traffickers issue to underage girls. On 10 September 2025 Kolkata Police's Anti-Human Trafficking Unit rescued ten people including nine minor girls from a house in Burtolla, North Kolkata, and arrested six people, including the couple running it (charged). The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers recruit significant numbers of Nepali and Bangladeshi women and girls for sex trafficking in India.

cases.title: Nepal child care homes — 'paper orphans' and recruitment by agents
cases.who: Child care homes (orphanages) in Nepal, many registered as NGOs; recruiting agents
cases.what: Nepal's National Child Rights Council counted 417 registered child care homes holding 10,905 children in 2021/22, and UNICEF estimates about 85% have a living parent or guardian. Agents take money from rural families with promises of schooling and are paid commissions by institutions; NGOs documented a child admitted on a forged parental death certificate. Researchers say homes use children to attract donations and that many operate unregistered. Only about 200 of 753 local governments had appointed the child welfare officers required by the Act Relating to Children (2018).

cases.title: Nepal — baby-buying in intercountry adoption; 2007 shutdown
cases.who: Orphanages and adoption intermediaries
cases.what: A Daily Telegraph investigation in March 2007 described baby-buying, bribes and deception of birth families. In April 2007 Nepal's new minister halted all intercountry adoptions, leaving about 400 Western families waiting; about 440 pending cases were processed after November 2007, and new rules were published in May 2008. UNICEF and Terre des hommes published 'Adopting: The Rights of the Child' in August 2008. Wikipedia records that the US later suspended adoptions of children declared abandoned because documents were unreliable.

cases.title: Nepal → India — trafficking of girls to Indian brothels (estimates)
cases.who: Trafficking networks recruiting via false job, marriage and online romance offers
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers use job offers and online romance scams to recruit Nepali women and children to India for sex trafficking; Nepali courts convicted 406 traffickers (231 for sex trafficking) in the year. A 2024 study it cites found a majority of workers in Nepal's adult entertainment sector were sex-trafficking victims, nearly half of them children. Research collated on Wikipedia gives estimates of 5,000–10,000 Nepali women and girls trafficked to India each year across a 1,850 km open border.
cases.cover_up: US TIP 2025: serious concerns of official complicity; traffickers bribe some Indian officials to fly Nepali workers to third countries.

cases.title: Kamathipura, Mumbai — red-light district fed by trafficking from Nepal and Indian states
cases.who: Brothels of Kamathipura
cases.what: Kamathipura, Mumbai's oldest and largest red-light district and one of Asia's largest, was established over 150 years ago under British rule; the BBC in 2013 put its sex workers at an estimated 20,000. Girls were trafficked there from poor villages in other Indian states, some as young as 11, on promises of domestic work. The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report is cited, though it could not be opened for this map, for a shift of sex trafficking in India toward spas, hotels and private residences, and for 2022 crime-data figures of 204 convicted traffickers and 1,134 acquittals; that report could not be opened in this pass (state.gov blocked).

flows.title: Canada → Nepal (aid-worker offender)
flows.what: A Canadian humanitarian working with street children abused boys at his home in Nepal.

networks.name: Orphanage trafficking and orphanage tourism (recruitment of children into institutions for donations)
networks.what: A recurring pattern in which orphanages are set up or kept full to attract foreign donations, volunteers and tourists, recruiting children who mostly have living parents, sometimes with payments to families or forged documents. patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: New Zealand → Papua New Guinea: priests sent after allegations.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

flows.title: New Zealand → Papua New Guinea: priests sent after allegations
flows.what: New Zealand's Royal Commission into Abuse in Care (2024) found the church transferred abusers to other ministries and recommended an investigation into Catholic priests sent to Papua New Guinea after abuse allegations. Numbers not stated.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2004: EU accession scrutiny and 2004 ban on intercountry adoption from Romania.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 21,188 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (7% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: 764 network — founder sentenced to 80 years
cases.who: 764 (online network on Discord/Telegram; founder Bradley Cadenhead)
cases.what: 764, named after the first digits of the ZIP code of Stephenville, Texas, extorted minors into producing abuse material, self-harm and animal cruelty. Its founder, Bradley Cadenhead, was arrested in August 2021 aged 16 and on 16 May 2023 was sentenced in Texas to 80 years after pleading guilty to nine counts of possession/promotion of child sexual abuse material. The US DOJ describes 764 as a nihilistic violent extremist network and its Counterterrorism Section prosecutes it; on 29 April 2025 DOJ announced the arrests of two alleged leaders of the subgroup '764 Inferno', in North Carolina and in Greece. On 10 December 2025 Canada became the first country to list 764 as a terrorist entity.

cases.title: Romania — post-1989 adoption trade and 2004 ban
cases.who: Private adoption agencies and intermediaries; Romanian authorities
cases.what: After Ceaușescu's fall, television images of about 100,000 children in orphanages led to an adoption boom; private agencies charged €7,500–25,000 and the system 'quickly became awash in corruption' (DW). Romania halted adoptions in June 1991 and, under EU pressure, passed a law in June 2004 banning all foreign adoptions except by grandparents. The European Parliament's rapporteur Baroness Emma Nicholson had criticised 'international adoption and child trafficking' in Romania. Romania's own HCCH return shows 458 intercountry adoptions in 2002, 332 in 2003, 2 in 2005 and 0 in 2006.

cases.title: Romanian state orphanages under Ceaușescu and after 1989
cases.who: Romanian state orphanages and institutions for disabled children
cases.what: Decree 770 (1966) banned abortion, and many children born afterwards were abandoned in state institutions, where they suffered neglect, physical and sexual abuse and sedation; physical and sexual abuse was reported to be common at the Siret children's psychiatric hospital. After 1989 large numbers of children were adopted abroad amid corruption and irregularities, and in 2004, under EU pressure, Romania banned international adoption except by grandparents. A 2009 BBC investigation found poor conditions persisted in some institutions.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Galați/Brăila — 'loverboy' ring exploiting minors in Western Europe (2021)
cases.who: Four suspects detained by DIICOT/BCCO
cases.what: In February 2021 Romanian organised-crime police and DIICOT prosecutors searched eight addresses in Galați and Brăila and detained four suspects for human trafficking, trafficking of minors and pimping. Investigators said that from August 2013 the group recruited girls and young women by the 'loverboy' method, hid minors in intermediate lodgings until they turned 18, then exploited them in Western Europe, earning about €350,000; nine victims, minor and adult, had been identified.

cases.title: Romania–UK 'loverboy' network dismantled — 21 arrested (Eurojust, 2020)
cases.who: Romanian organized criminal group using the 'loverboy' method
cases.what: On 9 September 2020 a Romanian–UK Joint Investigation Team supported by Eurojust arrested 21 members of a hierarchical group active since 2009 that seduced vulnerable Romanian girls with false promises of relationships, exploited minors in prostitution in Romania until they turned 18, and then moved them to the UK, Ireland and Germany. Thirty-two house searches were carried out (23 in Romania, 9 in the UK). Eurojust said Romania and the UK had cooperated in 76 trafficking investigations in four years.

cases.title: Bosnia — trafficking of women and girls; IPTF monitors and SFOR/DynCorp contractors
cases.who: Traffickers and bar owners; local Bosnian police; UN International Police Task Force (IPTF) monitors; US SFOR civilian contractors (DynCorp)
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's November 2002 report 'Hopes Betrayed' documented women and girls trafficked mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine into post-war Bosnia and held in debt bondage in bars and brothels. Local police were found acting as owners, guards and clients; 18 IPTF monitors who purchased women, visited brothels or faced trafficking-related charges went home, and none was confirmed prosecuted. A US Army CID report documented DynCorp contractors buying women from brothels; one confessed to buying a woman (with an Uzi) for 1,600 Deutschmarks. On 2 August 2002 a British employment tribunal unanimously found DynCorp had unfairly dismissed IPTF monitor Kathryn Bolkovac after she reported the trafficking.
cases.cover_up: Immunity: IPTF monitors were repatriated rather than prosecuted (18 returned home; HRW found no prosecution by Nov 2002); DynCorp contractors were sent home, preventing their use as witnesses; DynCorp fired whistleblower Kathryn Bolkovac in April 2001.

cases.title: Kosovo — trafficking for forced prostitution and the international presence (Amnesty 2004)
cases.who: Criminal networks; demand from NATO KFOR soldiers, UN police and international staff
cases.what: Amnesty International's May 2004 report said Kosovo had become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution since NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in 1999, with the international presence generating 80% of traffickers' income at the time. Women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia via Serbia, and local girls were also abducted. The UN peacekeeping department acknowledged in 2004 that peacekeepers had 'come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution'.
cases.cover_up: Amnesty found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries.

cases.title: Romania — girls in state institutions at risk; victims sent across Europe (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers; staff of some government-run institutions
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says most identified victims are women and girls exploited in Romania and in Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK; children in government-run institutions, particularly girls in homes for persons with disabilities, are at risk of sex trafficking; and Roma children as young as 11 are 'sold' into marriage. Courts convicted 161 traffickers (143 for sex trafficking) and 600 victims were identified in 2024.
cases.cover_up: Alleged complicity, misconduct and negligence by government employees in cases involving children in government-run homes remained a concern.

patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Mission or crisis zone where children were abused
patterns.role_note: AMISOM bases, Mogadishu — rape and sexual exploitation (HRW 2014).
patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that Sri Lankan peacekeepers had abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007, and 114 soldiers were sent home; none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014 and 2015; French judges closed the case against the French soldiers in 2018 without charges. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. In 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria, and 82 were still captive in 2024. The Lord's Resistance Army abducted children in Uganda and the neighbouring countries over many years; in 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

cases.who: Al-Shabaab; also Somali National Army, police, Ethiopian Liyu Police, clan militias
cases.what: The UN verified the abduction of 887 children in Somalia in 2024, 850 by Al-Shabaab, mainly for recruitment. cases.title: AMISOM bases, Mogadishu — rape and sexual exploitation (HRW 2014)
cases.who: African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) Ugandan and Burundian contingents
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's report of 8 September 2014, based on 50 interviews including 21 survivors, documented 10 incidents of sexual abuse, including rape and sexual assault, and 14 cases of sexual exploitation by African Union (AMISOM) soldiers, mainly Ugandan personnel at and around AMISOM's headquarters and Burundian personnel at their base in Mogadishu. Four rape cases and one sexual assault involved girls under 18; the youngest was a 12-year-old allegedly raped by a Ugandan soldier near Baidoa in May 2013. Many victims had gone to the bases to seek medicine or aid, including a woman seeking medicine for her sick baby, and interpreters facilitated soldiers' access; some women and girls were compelled into sex in exchange for money, food and medicine.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2007: scandal: Zoé's Ark members arrested trying to fly 103 children to France; convicted 26 December
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Chad — sexual violence against girls by the Chadian National Army (UN verified 2022).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers.
