patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found West and Central Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Chad — Zoé's Ark tries to fly 103 children to France (convicted 2007)
cases.who: French charity L'Arche de Zoé (founder Éric Breteau)
cases.what: In October 2007 members of the French charity Zoé's Ark were detained in Chad as they tried to fly 103 children to France; the charity said they were orphans from Sudan's Darfur region, but authorities found most were from Chad and not orphans. On 26 December 2007 a Chadian court convicted six French members of attempting to kidnap the children and sentenced them to eight years' forced labour, and ordered each to pay €60,000 to each of the 103 children; a Chadian and a Sudanese defendant got four years and two Chadians were acquitted. The six were transferred to France, and Chad's President Idriss Déby pardoned them at the end of March 2008.

cases.title: Chad — sexual violence against girls by the Chadian National Army (UN verified 2022)
cases.who: Chadian National Army
cases.what: The UN verified rape and other sexual violence against three girls by the Chadian National Army in Lac Province in 2022, and in Sudan attributed 4 of 35 cases of sexual violence against girls aged 12 to 17 to the Chadian National Army. In the Lake Chad basin it verified the abduction of 191 children in Lac Province and Diffa.

cases.title: Central African Republic — Deschamps panel finds 'gross institutional failure' by the UN over child abuse by foreign troops (2015)
cases.who: French Sangaris forces; Chadian and Equatorial Guinean MISCA soldiers; UN officials who handled the allegations
cases.what: The External Independent Review Panel appointed by the Secretary-General and chaired by Marie Deschamps reported on 17 December 2015. It examined accounts by boys aged about 8 to 13 sheltering at the M'Poko camp in Bangui that soldiers, largely from the French Sangaris force, and also Chadian and Equatorial Guinean MISCA troops, had sexually abused them between December 2013 and June 2014, often in exchange for food or money. It called the UN's handling a 'gross institutional failure' and found that three senior UN officials had abused their authority.
cases.cover_up: Report passed 'from inbox to inbox'; panel found abuse of authority by the head of MINUSCA's Human Rights and Justice Section, the SRSG for MINUSCA and the head of OIOS, and that staff became more concerned with whether the allegations had been improperly leaked to French authorities than with acting on them

networks.what: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. cases.title: Thailand — 'Baby 101' surrogate baby-breeding operation
cases.who: Baby 101 company
cases.what: In February 2011 Thai police freed 14 Vietnamese women, half of them pregnant, held in two Bangkok houses with passports confiscated by a company called Baby 101 that took orders from childless couples for newborns. A Taiwanese woman said to run the operation was charged with human trafficking; four said they had been tricked, and the health minister said some appeared to have been raped.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2023: US Virgin Islands government suits against the Epstein estate and JPMorgan.
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

cases.title: US Virgin Islands government suits — Epstein estate and JPMorgan
cases.who: Epstein estate; JPMorgan Chase; Deutsche Bank
cases.what: Epstein owned the private island of Little St. James in the US Virgin Islands. The territory's government reached a $105m settlement with Epstein's estate and a $62.5m settlement with billionaire Leon Black. In December 2022 it sued JPMorgan Chase, claiming the bank ignored warning signs and facilitated Epstein's activities; JPMorgan agreed in June 2023 to pay $290m to nearly 200 Epstein victims in a class action and in September 2023 to pay the Virgin Islands $75m. The settlements carried no criminal findings.
cases.cover_up: Banks were alleged to have facilitated and concealed the operation by keeping Epstein as a client. New York's financial regulator fined Deutsche Bank $150m in July 2020 for ignoring red flags on Epstein. UK regulators permanently banned former JPMorgan banker Jes Staley (upheld June 2025) for recklessly misleading them about his Epstein relationship.

cases.title: Ankara prosecutors' inquiry into alleged trafficking of girls from Turkey to Epstein
cases.who: Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor's Office (inquiry)
cases.what: On 23 Dec 2025 Ankara prosecutors reportedly opened an inquiry after opposition MP Turhan Çömez cited the DOJ files. The underlying document is a May 2009 civil complaint by 'Jane Doe No. 102' alleging 'upon information and belief' that Epstein brought minor girls from 'Turkey, the Czech Republic, Asia, and numerous other countries'. Prosecutors are reviewing the files; no findings or charges have been reported.

networks.name: Jeffrey Epstein and associates
networks.what: Financier Jeffrey Epstein (d. 2019) and Ghislaine Maxwell (convicted 2021) sexually abused and trafficked girls, some as young as 14, between at least 1994 and 2005 across homes in New York, Palm Beach, New Mexico, the US Virgin Islands, Paris and London. Model agent Jean-Luc Brunel was charged in France and died in custody. Banks paid hundreds of millions in settlements. 2025–2026 file releases led to misconduct and corruption inquiries against officials in the UK and Norway.
